arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: The government argued that the Vaccine Act does not provide for an award of attorneys' fees on a petition that is denied as untimely.
the side that brought the case argued that Section 15(e)(1) makes any petition filed under Section 11 eligible for fees, even if denied, provided two conditions are met.
Justice Ginsburg asked whether the parties file anything in the Federal Register.

Chief Justice Roberts asked if the side that brought the case's conclusion is that the deadline is not jurisdictional. He later asked if the Court should say a deadline is jurisdictional if it sounds that way to secure a win. Justice Kagan asked if the Department subtracts untimely petitions from its congressional reports. Justice Sotomayor noted the government concedes the deadline is not jurisdictional.

paragraphs: The case tests the scope of the Vaccine Act fee provision. The government argues the statute bars fees for untimely filings. the side that brought the case argues the statute allows fees even when a court denies a late claim.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case determines whether attorneys can recover fees when a court dismisses a vaccine injury claim for being late. The outcome affects the financial risk lawyers take when filing these claims. It also shapes how the government reports untimely petitions to Congress. The ruling clarifies the scope of the Vaccine Act fee provision for all future cases.
